1. The Democratic Party’s elected officials, staffers, and donors are on average very progressive compared not only to the median voter but to most of the rank and file people who vote for Democrats.

Baldur’s Gate 3 and Mass Effect were almost certainly made primarily by Democrat voters, and some of the scenarios reflect that, but they are both games that put choices in the player’s hand rather than dictating things or lecturing the player.

Mass Effect is about how these choices are difficult.  It’s about a universe of alien races who have very recently been at all-out war with each other, who have deep enmities based on real and serious grievances, and must figure out how to unite against a Cthulhu who is coming to eat them all. 

The universe is full of killer robots and giant spiders and savage lizard people who multiply like a virus, and you have to dare to trust them all if you want to defeat the thing that is coming to kill everybody. Obviously this is an allegory about war and racism and obviously it is not pro war or pro racism.

But what makes it really great and resonant is that it recognizes that uniting with people who are different isn’t always easy. It recognizes that these different people might have fundamental values that are at odds with your own, or that you may have good reasons to be hesitant to trust them. It doesn’t treat diverse coexistence as a natural state of society. Maybe purely as a function of being 15 years old, it is very unwoke in many regards.

Meanwhile, “Dragon Age: The Veilguard” spends multiple hours talking about nonbinary identity and pronouns. So the “BioWare has always been woke” claims really don’t hold up.
